developer: The person driving the whole process from the very first step: writing code, testing it locally, and starting the cycle everything else follows from.
ideation: Where the idea for the project takes shape: what problem it solves, who it's for, and whether it's worth building before any code gets written.
architecture: Deciding how the pieces of the system fit together: what components exist, how they talk to each other, and where the boundaries between them sit.
tech-stack-locked-in: Choosing the languages, frameworks, and tools the project will actually be built with, and committing to them so development time isn't spent re-litigating the choice later.
writing-the-code: The actual implementation: turning the architecture and the chosen stack into working code.
local-testing: Running every check available on the developer's own machine before the code goes anywhere shared: unit tests, linters, formatters, type checks, and a local build.
fail: The point where local checks either pass or don't. A failure sends the code back for fixes; a pass moves it toward being pushed.
debug-fix-code: Fixing whatever a failed local check flagged, then re-running the checks until they pass.
commit-push-code: A push in Git is the operation of uploading local commits from your machine to a remote repository, updating it with your latest changes.
github: Storing the code in a GitHub repository, where it becomes visible and shareable beyond the developer's own machine.
open-pull-request: A pull request (PR) on GitHub is a collaborative feature that allows you to propose changes to a project's codebase and ask others to review and approve them before they are merged into the main project.
pull-request-merged:
Once the PR is approved and merged, the change becomes part of the shared main branch, which is what actually kicks off the next phase.

This merge is the event that starts the CI pipeline automatically. No one manually starts a build; the merge itself fires it.
checkout-source-code: The first thing the CI pipeline does: pull the exact commit being tested out of version control onto a clean machine.
ci-system: A Machine / Server. The tool actually running the pipeline, such as Jenkins, GitHub Actions, or GitLab CI/CD. Different projects use different ones, but the job is the same: orchestrate the stages that follow.
install-dependencies: Installing exactly what the project declares it needs, on the clean CI machine, rather than relying on whatever happens to be cached locally.
build-the-application: Compiling or bundling the project into a form that can actually run.
security-scan-sast: Static Application Security Testing: scanning the source code itself for security issues and unsafe patterns, without running it.
run-unit-tests: Testing individual functions or components in isolation to confirm they behave as expected.
run-integration-tests: Testing how multiple parts of the system work together, which unit tests alone can't catch.
code-coverage-check: Measuring how much of the codebase was actually exercised by the tests that just ran.
store-artifact-in-registry: Once everything passes, the build output gets packaged and stored somewhere it can be pulled from later, unchanged, by every later stage.
task-failed: If any CI stage fails, the pipeline stops here instead of continuing forward with a broken build.
pipeline-stops-ci: The CI run halts immediately on failure, rather than letting later stages run against something already broken.
developer-fixes-ci: Someone fixes whatever the pipeline flagged, then commits and pushes again, which restarts the CI process on the new code.
cd-system: Picks up the artifact that passed CI and carries it forward through delivery or deployment.
manual-approval-gate: Whether a human needs to approve the release before it proceeds. If yes, that's delivery; if no, it moves automatically, which is deployment.
pipeline-stops-cd: If the release is rejected at the approval gate, it goes no further.
fetch-build-artifacts: Retrieving the exact artifact that passed CI, so nothing gets rebuilt or substituted along the way.
inject-config-secrets: Adding environment-specific configuration and credentials at deploy time, rather than baking them into the artifact itself.
package-container-image: Wrapping the built application into a container image, ready to be stored and run consistently anywhere.
push-image-docker-hub: Uploading that container image to a registry, so later stages can pull the exact same image rather than rebuilding it.
pull-image-and-deploy: Pulling that stored image back down and running it in the target environment.
staging-server: An environment built to resemble production closely enough that problems show up here first, before real users ever see them.
run-smoke-tests: Quick checks confirming the deployment actually came up and responds at all, separate from testing whether its logic is correct.
run-health-check: Confirming the deployed service is actually healthy and running, not just that it started.
all-checks-pass: Whether staging cleared every check. A pass moves toward production; a failure sends it back to the developer.
notify-developer-team: Alerting whoever's responsible that something failed, whether that's a staging check or a production health check further down the line.
developer-fixes-cd: Addressing whatever staging flagged, then sending the fix back through the CD system rather than starting over from scratch.
deployment-strategy: The method chosen for actually rolling the new version out to production: Blue-Green, Canary, Rolling, or Recreate, each with different tradeoffs around rollback speed and how many users are exposed at once.
automated-manual-deployment-production: The new version actually goes live, either fully automatically or with a person triggering the release.
post-production-health-check: Confirming the newly deployed version is actually healthy in production itself, not just in staging. A failure triggers rollback.
rollback: Reverting to the last known-good version when the post-production health check fails, rather than trying to fix the problem live.
end-users: The people the whole pipeline exists to serve. This is where the new version actually reaches them.
notify-team-success: Confirmation back to the team that the release went out cleanly.
monitoring-observability: Ongoing collection of metrics, logs, and traces from the running system, catching problems that only show up over time, well after the deployment finished.
